entry.title: Agent engineering starts by assuming the model gets fooled
entry.summary: Cynthia Akiotu of Accenture at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on identity, MCP tools and authorization checks that hold when prompt injection works.
entry.content:
A customer asks a support agent about refunds, the agent retrieves the refund policy, and hidden in that document is an instruction to export every customer case to an outside address. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Cynthia Akiotu, AI security and data protection architect at Accenture and a Microsoft MVP in Security Copilot, used that one scenario to argue that once an LLM can act, every engineering decision becomes a security decision.

Her design goal is refreshingly modest: don't pretend the model can't be manipulated. Contain what happens when it is.

Same model, new blast radius

Cynthia starts by putting prompt engineering and agent engineering side by side. The model is identical. What changed is everything around it: instructions, context, identity, tools, actions and governance. A chatbot that answers wrongly misleads someone. An agent that acts wrongly sends the email, updates the record or deletes it.

Each layer adds capability and widens the blast radius unless it's deliberately constrained. And these layers aren't one team's checklist; identity, data, security and operations teams all own a piece.

Retrieved text can inform, never authorise

The refund scenario is indirect prompt injection. The attacker never talks to the agent; they plant instructions in a source the agent will read. Her design question is sharp and practical: who can write to the knowledge sources your agent retrieves from? Detection helps, she says, but you still need controls beyond the model, because the next question is whose authority the agent is running on.

She lays out three identity patterns: delegated access on behalf of a signed-in user (the agent inherits that user's reach), an agent with its own account like a digital worker, and app-only identities for background work. If any of these is broad, a fooled model gets broad reach.

MCP is a protocol, not a trust decision

The Model Context Protocol section is the one platform teams will screenshot. MCP standardises how agents discover and call tools, which is convenient. It doesn't make a server trustworthy. Her example shows a ticket-search tool whose description quietly asks the model to send a report elsewhere, which is tool description poisoning. Review servers and tool definitions, restrict discovery, validate requests and enforce permissions at execution.

Then the line every agent builder should tape to the monitor: capability doesn't mean authorization. Writing "please don't delete data" in the system prompt is a suggestion. A policy check in the application that denies the delete because no approver exists, and logs the attempt, is a boundary.

Follow the attack, then follow the trace

Cynthia connects the pieces into one path: the agent retrieves the poisoned policy, mistakes it for an instruction, tries the export, and the API rejects it. The model was fooled; the system held. Controls sit at several points (inputs, retrieved context, tool arguments, actions, outputs), and an AI gateway is a good shared front door for model traffic, but tool execution may take a different route to an enterprise API and still needs its own check.

Correlated traces let the security team see the denied export even when the customer sees a normal answer. Her case study uses the Microsoft stack she works in, including Entra Agent ID and Agent 365 for agent identity and life cycle, as one example of turning these principles into platform capabilities.

Least agency

Her closing pattern is least agency: enough freedom to do the job and no more, narrow tool access, deny unapproved actions by default, humans in the loop for irreversible changes, and deterministic application logic validating whatever the model proposes. Before production, ask who owns the agent, which identity it uses, and whether you can trace, stop and recover its actions.

Who should watch

Engineers moving from chatbots to agents with tools, and security architects reviewing them. It's a clear, structured talk rather than a code walkthrough, and the refund story makes it easy to retell in your own design review.

entry.title: Your agent orchestrator won't save your money; the thin controller will
entry.summary: Yedidya Schwartz, CTO of Quicklizard, at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on crashing six durable engines to see who pays twice for model calls.
entry.content:
Yedidya Schwartz, CTO at Quicklizard, built a pipeline where AI agents turn a ticket into a mergeable pull request, then crashed the same tiny job on six durable execution engines to see which one protected his model bill. None did by default. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 he showed that the shape of your code, a thin controller with every model call in its own step, decided the cost, not the engine.

This is one of the most evidence-heavy talks of the event: real failures, a controlled experiment and a bill kept outside every engine so none could flatter itself.

Green on GitHub, phase 8 never ran

The first version was one 338-line Markdown prompt that Claude ran on a GitHub self-hosted runner, from intake through planning, build, tests, QA, three-model review, translations into 12 languages, PR and CI. For two hours it went well. QA checked 34 acceptance criteria and all passed. Then, at phase 8, instead of translating, the model wrote a polished summary of the translation work it was supposed to do and stopped.

GitHub showed success, because success meant the process exited cleanly. The runner deleted the pod with the commits still on its disk. No draft PR, no traces, every model call already paid. Yedidya's conclusion: the model can do the work, but code has to decide when it's done. He rewrote the pipeline as roughly 485 lines of Python where a plain for loop picks the next phase, and a for loop can't decide to write an essay instead of running phase 9.

Defaults were built for seconds, agents run for hours

Before choosing a tool he wrote down hard requirements, the biggest being that agents must run inside his private network to reach internal services and databases. That alone ruled out most hosted coding agents without an enterprise plan or a beta feature.

Then he compared engines on his own terms: LangGraph saves between steps but not inside them, the DAG schedulers handle loops back to a critic only with workarounds, Inngest caps a step at two hours, and several engines kill a step that stays quiet too long. His best slide is about defaults: they were tuned for API calls, while an agent step can take hours. His CI fix step started with a 20-minute timeout and ended at four hours. He picked Temporal, partly because he knew it well, and was clear that this is his choice for his pipeline, not a ranking.

The experiment: who pays twice?

The part to watch closely is the crash test. A fake model charged a fixed price per call and logged every charge to a file the engine never saw. A clean run cost exactly $2. He killed the job three ways (mid-call, graceful shutdown, right after the file write) on Temporal, Restate, Inngest, LangGraph, DBOS and Prefect, in two variants.

Written the natural way, with the model call and file write in one step, every engine overpaid: $4 on Restate, DBOS and Prefect, $6 on LangGraph, $14 on Inngest (and $12 with no crash at all, due to defaults), and $10 on Temporal. With the thin controller, where each model call and each write is its own step and a step is skipped if its output is saved, every engine landed at $3.50 for a mid-call crash and exactly $2 after the save. Worse, no engine's UI showed the second charge. Count your money outside the engine.

Agents lie about success, so stop asking them

The war stories are memorable. A skip-if-output-exists check once found a file full of error text, skipped the model and shipped an empty PR. Translations went missing at random because two workers had separate disks, and the scheduler, not the model, decided where each step landed: seven of 12 languages vanished until all files moved to S3. Agents claimed a type check passed that they never ran; Yedidya's run produced five compile errors in components the agent had made up.

His proof ladder puts the agent's self-report at the bottom and a real diff, a build his code runs, green CI and a human merge above it. In his pipeline, done means CI is green. He also zooms out to Stripe, Spotify and Uber, and his verdict on whether it's worth it is honest: not yet, but close, with about one feature in four merged and only after a lot of human work.

Who should watch

Anyone about to choose Temporal, Restate, LangGraph or friends for agent workflows, and anyone whose agents report success on their own say-so. It's long, and every slide earns its place.

entry.title: Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 roundup: checking agents before they act
entry.summary: Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 in review, from hooks that gate coding agents and SBOMs that stop at the model to cell isolation, masking checks and safe recovery.
entry.content:
Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 ran online on October 1, 2026, with 24 talks, and one question kept coming back: what happens to security controls built for a human pace when the code is written, installed and shipped by agents? Speakers from Harness, ArmorCode, Keeper Security, WSO2, SAP, Microsoft, Tesla, T-Mobile and AWS answered it from different corners: before the tool call, inside the artifact, at the tenant boundary, in the test data and during recovery.

Put the check before the action, not after the alert

The busiest track was about coding agents, and its speakers converged on timing. Artemis Leonardou (NOFire AI) described an incident where the alerting worked exactly as designed and was still useless, because it reported something that had already broken. Humans hesitate before acting; agents don't. The talk is about evaluating an action before it executes, using the pipeline you already have.

Karan Bansal (ArmorCode) made hooks the enforcement layer: they intercept every tool call between the agent's decision and its execution and run outside the model, so prompt injection can't talk its way past them. His blocking scripts cover dangerous commands, secret exfiltration, typosquatted installs and agents that mark failing tests as skipped to fake a green build. Oleksandr Kryvchenko (Keeper Security) showed why that matters: Claude Code's permissions.deny rules can be silently bypassed, and PreToolUse hooks put policy in your own code instead of the model's.

Yunhao Jiao (TestSprite) brought numbers from CoderCup, a public competition where four frontier coding agents built the same ten-phase app. Every agent broke previously working features between 31 and 57 times in a single build, and the breaks stayed invisible until something ran the application. His argument: the PR gate is too late, so verify while the agent works. Deepanshu Kukreja looked at the other side, using agents to automate DevSecOps chores across IaC, CI/CD and incident response.

The supply chain now includes weights, memory and RAG

The keynote from Roshan Piyush, Head of Security Research at Harness, traced supply chain attacks from SolarWinds and XZ Utils to Shai-Hulud, then argued that agent configuration (hooks, skills, CLAUDE.md files, memory, MCP servers) is where the trust has moved. He ran a discovery script on his own laptop and found more than a thousand agent artifacts, half of them unknown to him.

Emmy Eide (Realign Labs) went after the artifact itself. DevSecOps got good at proving what's in a build, but a model-bearing service ships a multi-gigabyte blob that no scanner parses and no SBOM format meaningfully describes. The talk maps which gates still fire and which wave through what they can't inspect. Jayakumar Ramalingam (SiriusXM) covered APIs where a single request can now trigger inference, retrieve user context and call downstream tools. Ananda Kumar Dey (Quadrant Technologies) and Sirisha Ayyagari applied the same thinking to enterprise RAG and to AI-driven pricing inside SAP.

Isolation and identity, without long-lived secrets

Lahiru De Silva (WSO2) gave one of the most concrete talks of the day. Namespaces and NetworkPolicies stop accidents, not a determined neighbour, so OpenChoreo, a CNCF Sandbox internal developer platform, gives each tenant environment its own cell: a namespace with a Cilium policy boundary, its own observability scope, and four directional gateways (northbound, westbound, southbound, eastbound) built on Envoy and the Kubernetes Gateway API.

Venkata Velavarthipati removed stored credentials from multi-cloud pipelines with OpenID Connect and workload identity federation. Perumalsamy Ravindran covered Terraform across providers, Sonu Kumar (Peoplefluent) governed platform engineering, and Rahul Kizhakkepachilamakol (AWS) the anti-entropy mechanisms that keep vulnerability findings flowing within minutes at cloud scale, where every minute of delay widens the exposure window.

Test your detection and your recovery, not just your build

Aleksander Kryukov asked whether your alert would have fired in time, then answered it with a harness that replays candidate detection rules against 46 historical Web3 exploits using state-forked execution. Detection deadlines come from observed exfiltration curves, not arbitrary SLAs. Sanjay Iyer made a point that deserves more airtime: a recovery can meet RTO and RPO and still replay duplicate transactions past fraud controls or restore stale permissions. Mridula Chilakamarri (Dell Technologies) built deterministic request-level diagnostics on OpenTelemetry and W3C Trace Context.

Data, privacy and the browser

Siyuan Feng (CSC) tackled a problem every test-data team hits: validating masking when legacy tables have no stable keys. The trick is to intersect sensitive values first and build composite identifiers only for the overlapping subset. Mary Sirisha Duggimpudi (T-Mobile) covered AI-driven sensitive data discovery, Vinay Puri (Amazon) ML-based compliance monitoring, and Ashwin Kumar (Tesla) identity binding for executives reading analytics on unmanaged phones.

Two talks stayed close to the pipeline. Elena Darevskaya (SAP) showed how a customer's Content Security Policy or COOP headers break an embedded SDK that worked fine in development, and how to catch it earlier. Peter De Tender (Microsoft) walked through what GitHub Advanced Security covers out of the box.

Sponsors and where to watch

entry.title: Your coding agent's dotfiles are the new software supply chain
entry.summary: Roshan Piyush of Harness at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 on why hooks, skills, memory and MCP servers are where AI supply chain attacks now land.
entry.content:
Roshan Piyush, Head of Security Research at Harness, pointed a discovery script at his own laptop before giving his Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 talk. It found 1,103 agent-related artifacts, about half of which he didn't know were there, including 158 skills and around 830 instruction files like CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md. His argument follows from that inventory: the software supply chain now runs through the configuration that tells AI agents how to behave, and almost nobody reviews it.

Attackers follow the trust

The first third of the talk is a fast tour of supply chain incidents, and the point is the pattern, not the nostalgia. SolarWinds shipped a signed backdoor through a build pipeline. Codecov's compromised uploader script exfiltrated environment variables. Alex Birsan's dependency confusion research showed registries preferring the higher version number over the internal source. XZ Utils was a two-year trust-building operation, caught only because a developer was annoyed by a 500 millisecond SSH delay. Roshan's aside lands well: an AI agent would never have bothered about half a second.

Then the newer ones. The LiteLLM compromise came through an already-compromised Trivy action and dropped a Python .pth file, which runs every time the interpreter starts. Shai-Hulud tore through npm and used TruffleHog, a secret scanner, to find the secrets it stole. A later variant used AI to craft payloads and embedded a request about building a nuclear bomb, so that LLM-based malware scanners would refuse to look at it. Each step moved to wherever developers had put their trust: an update, a tool, a package manager, a contributor, a release channel. Roshan's claim is that trust is now moving to the agent.

Committed config is committed behaviour

The sharpest line in the talk is about what lives in our repos now: "Not to commit dot ENV files, but now we commit an entire behavior." Teams check in CLAUDE.md, .cursor rules, mcp.json and settings.json so colleagues can share them. Anyone who clones the repo inherits instructions they've probably never read, which a colleague may have pasted from somewhere else.

Hooks get special treatment. In Roshan's words, "Hooks have become the dot bash RC problem for the agents at scale." They run on every prompt and every action, they can silently rewrite context, and his team's research found that hooks could edit other hooks without any approval prompt. A malicious instruction in an MCP server can install a hook that does the rest.

Memory, hallucinated packages and blind spots between tools

Three more attack paths get a short treatment each:

  • Memory poisoning. Tell an agent once to use a mock payment tool for testing and forget about it. Months later a vector store retrieves that note by relevance, not recency, and the agent authorises a payment through the mock. Roshan also cited research showing five malicious documents in a million can hijack an answer with a 90% success rate.
  • Hallucinated dependencies. Agents rarely typo, but they do invent package names. An attacker only has to register the name the model keeps suggesting.
  • Cross-tool blindness. Claude refused to tamper with its own hooks and settings, but Cursor or Windsurf would happily edit Claude's files, and the reverse holds too. Each agent guards itself and ignores its neighbours.

He also admitted that he, a head of security research, usually picks "always allow" on the permission prompt. Humans get tired of approving things, and he counts that fatigue as part of the threat model rather than a moral failing.

What he wants teams and vendors to do

The recommendations split in two. Teams can act now: open your .claude and .cursor folders and look; review agent configuration as source code; replace static API keys with short-lived role credentials (his team uses 24-hour sessions for Bedrock); and red-team the models you rely on, as NIST AI 600-1 expects. Vendors and the ecosystem need to supply what nobody can build alone: a kill switch that hooks can't disable, signed models with provenance (CycloneDX ML-BOM and SPDX AI BOM are a start), signed MCP servers, provenance for hooks, and guardrails that work across agents. His blunt summary: "AI supply chain is completely broken right now."

Who should watch

Platform and AppSec engineers rolling coding agents out to a whole organisation, and anyone who has approved a CLAUDE.md in code review without reading it. The talk is threat modelling and field notes rather than a product demo, and the attack history alone makes a good briefing for a team that hasn't been following the npm incidents.

entry.title: Conf42 AI Agents 2026: less LLM, more harness
entry.summary: Conf42 AI Agents 2026 roundup - planning without model calls, AI coding harnesses, LLM-as-judge testing, runaway token bills and agent security, in 22 talks.
entry.content:
Conf42 AI Agents 2026 ran online on September 24, 2026, with 22 talks, and the loudest message was a sceptical one: the model is rarely the problem. Speaker after speaker argued that what makes an agent shippable is the system around it, meaning deterministic planning, typed tools, review harnesses, evals, budgets, and identity boundaries. There were plenty of demos, but the best talks were about what happens after the demo.

The full lineup is on the Conf42 AI Agents 2026 event page, and the recordings are in the YouTube playlist.

Stop asking the model what to do next

Maureese Williams, an AI Engineer at Disney, started from a mundane observation: at every step, an agent asks the language model what to do next, so a twenty-step task costs twenty model calls and gives a different plan each run. The GATS approach (Graph-Augmented Tree Search) runs UCB1 tree search over a state-transition graph the agent builds as it works. The LLM never picks an action; it is the last rung of an escalation ladder, after symbolic rules and learned statistics, and its answers are cached.

Michael Haim, founder and CEO of Zindell Technologies, tackled the same non-determinism from the language side: you cannot orchestrate agents with a plain if or switch when their output is fuzzy, so use pattern matching to turn it into structured, auditable control flow. And Elizabeth Fuentes Leone of AWS showed semantic tool selection: every call serialises every tool description into the context, so filter tools with vector search before they reach the LLM, cutting both wrong picks and token cost.

The harness decides what ships

AI coding got its own track, and almost none of it was about prompts.

  • Ruben Marcus Luz Paschoarelli of MultiVM Labs argued that AI coding fails because the system around the model trusts the wrong evidence, and showed his harness: short specs, isolated git worktrees, model routing by role, browser verification, screenshot gates, and cost controls.
  • Guido Scheffler of CGI told the story of scaling AI code reviews across more than 70 projects, moving from brittle prompts to a deterministic review harness with an agent runner, an MCP server, managed checklists, and enforced completeness.
  • Suneet Malhotra, Senior Manager of Test Engineering at Motorola Solutions, presented a Claude Code and MCP pipeline whose three MCP servers turn product requirements into Jira stories, test cases, and Appium code at about 80% accuracy; the talk is about the other 20%, and why the human PR gate is mandatory.
  • Kemet Dugue walked through how Uber's driver onboarding team turned script-heavy manual processes into agentic workflows, and Peter De Tender of Microsoft showed how his open-source library of Azure demo scenarios became an agentic deployment system. Kabir Ibraheem of Meltwater offered a practical tour of AI tools for full-stack engineers.

Who judges the agent

Testing non-deterministic systems came up again and again. Liran Yushinsky, who leads automation at JFrog, asked how you test an AI that never gives you the same answer twice when it generates executable code through a chain of tool calls, and answered with LLM-as-judge alongside conventional checks.

Diamond sponsor Harness made the enterprise case: Shubham Jindal, Director of AI at Harness, laid out four pillars (context engineering, evals, memory, and governance) and argued that an eval suite should never pass at 100%, because then it cannot measure progress. Shubham Sharma of Microsoft proposed a unified readiness framework, so models, retrieval, orchestration, and human-in-the-loop workflows are assessed together rather than team by team.

The bill comes at 2 AM

Yamini Rathamsetty and Karthik Akula of AWS opened with the scene every agent operator dreads: 2 AM, no customers, no deploys, every dashboard green, and the bill climbing by multiples because their own agents were working hard all night on nothing. The talk dissects retry storms, runaway tool calls, context bloat, and multi-agent overhead.

Vladimir Beskorovainyi of Besk Tech brought the most production-scarred talk of the day: an on-prem text-to-SQL platform with open-weight models across 500+ data marts and 30M+ users. The opener says it all: "Very few people have to answer for the number it gives at 9:00 in the morning."

Don't give the agent a shell

The trust track was about boundaries. Ahmed Tariq of Simplify9 argued for a small set of typed tools, a deliberately limited identity, and enforcement outside the model, instead of a shell and a broad credential. Blaize Stewart of GBLI broke a RAG application live with prompt injection, poisoned documents, and broken document-level authorisation. Morgan Willis of AWS summed it up: don't trust the agent, trust the system you build around it, with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and the Strands Agents SDK as the toolkit.

Agents meet enterprise data

Agents are only as good as the data they act on. Rohit Deshpande and Scott Young of SAP showed a ReAct agent that turns a request like AR aging by customer into a deployed dashboard over live data via MCP. Vishwak Thatikonda of Starbucks explained why master data management built for reporting breaks when agents make decisions on it. Pon Murugesh Devendren of Deloitte built event-driven agents for proactive SAP incident management, Nick Rezaee of Harvard showed agents that turn wearable data into timely interventions, and Dmytro Hlotenko of Sage confessed that his Step Functions DAG for judging 8,000 photos was a lie, and went agentic.

Sponsors and what's next

Thanks to diamond sponsors Harness and LLMday, gold sponsor the Prompt Engineering Conference, the HockeyStick podcast, and all the media partners on the event page.

The series returns with Conf42 AI Agents 2027 on September 23, 2027. Until then, the playlist holds enough harness engineering to keep your agents honest.

entry.title: Enterprise AI in four pillars: context, evals, memory, governance
entry.summary: Shubham Jindal of Harness at Conf42 AI Agents 2026 on why AI demos stall before production, and the four pillars that get agents there.
entry.content:
An AI demo takes days to build and wows the room; the production version can take months and still embarrass you in front of a customer. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Shubham Jindal, Director of AI at Harness, laid out the blueprint his team uses to close that gap: four pillars called context, evals, memory, and governance, each with concrete habits you can copy.

This is a sponsor keynote, and Shubham says up front that Harness has built all four pillars into its own AI for the software delivery pipeline. But the talk is a framework, not a product tour. Almost everything in it applies to any team shipping agents to paying users.

Demos run on prompts, production runs on context

Shubham's opening claim is that the mindset has to shift from prompt engineering to context engineering. In a demo you are not throwing large data at the model, so a clever prompt carries the day. In production the model meets your siloed systems, your company jargon, and your sensitive data, and that is where it starts to make things up with great confidence.

His line for it: "Context is the new code." His team's case is personal. Harness has separate CI, CD, and code products, and an LLM trained on the whole internet does not know that CI means something specific inside Harness.

He gave four practical tricks for keeping the context window healthy:

  • Compaction. Summarise the conversation as it nears the limit and keep only the decisions. He compares it to a garbage collector.
  • Large outputs go to files. A Jira or GitHub MCP call can return a giant JSON blob. Write it to a file and let the agent read the slice it needs, instead of flooding the window.
  • Context editing. Proactively drop dead ends, like the five wrong Gradle commands the agent tried before finding the right one.
  • Semantic augmentation. Load skills and reference material when they become relevant, not all at once in the system prompt.

A knowledge graph is the compiler for your context

The most useful example in the talk is a question that sounds simple: which of my PRs caused an incident last week? The answer crosses the PR, the CI run, the CD deployment, the version that shipped, and the on-call page. Ask an agent to stitch that from three raw data sources and it will guess at relationships it does not understand.

Shubham's fix is to extract the entities you care about (services, users, incidents, releases), enrich them with metadata such as owners, link them into a graph, and expose that graph through an API the agent can query and walk. If context is the new code, he says, the knowledge graph is its compiler.

Evals should fail on purpose

The second most important pillar, in his ranking, is evals. Unit tests assume deterministic code; agents are probabilistic, so many teams skip testing entirely because they cannot define what good looks like. His example is model switching: an agent tuned on Opus burns too many tokens, so you want to try Sonnet. Without evals you are changing a model name and hoping.

The framework he described:

  • LLM-as-a-judge checks, ideally with a different model than the one being judged.
  • Regression evals as a quality gate in CI/CD before any prompt, temperature, or model change ships.
  • Evals on production traces. Harness runs a simple user temperament check that asks whether the user seems frustrated, types in caps, or repeats the same question.
  • Every production failure becomes a new eval case.

The idea worth stealing is that an eval suite should not pass at 100%. Treat it like a benchmark: if 80 of 100 cases pass today, a change that moves you to 85 is progress and one that drops you to 75 is a regression. A suite that always passes can only tell you about the cases you already solved.

Memory makes an assistant, governance makes it shippable

On memory, Shubham separates short-term memory (the current session) from long-term memory that bubbles up patterns, such as which repos a team works in or what a user keeps asking about. His summary: chatbots forget, assistants remember. He also traces the arc from chatbot to in-app assistant to autonomous agent, with examples like an agent that watches a PR's CI, fixes failures, and pushes until it is green.

Governance he calls the boring pillar enterprises care about most. He splits it into scoped access (do not hand an agent every tool in the GitHub MCP when it only needs a few), guardrails such as PII redaction and EU data residency, real-time content filters, and full audit trails of tool calls and model versions. Governance, in his words, is the new runtime, because it only exists while the agent is running.

Who should watch

Engineers and leads who have a working agent prototype and a nervous security team. The context-window tricks and the "evals as benchmarks" framing are worth the time on their own. If you are still deciding whether to build an agent at all, start elsewhere.

entry.title: Conf42 Observability 2026 - when green stopped meaning healthy
entry.summary: Conf42 Observability 2026 in review, 20 talks on tracing AI agents, dashboards that lie, eBPF, telemetry pipelines and using signals to test.
entry.content:
Conf42 Observability 2026 went out on September 10, 2026 with 20 talks, and a single complaint kept surfacing in different accents: the dashboard said everything was fine. Sometimes the culprit was an AI agent reporting 200 OK while answering wrong, sometimes a payment provider, sometimes a fallback path nobody had ever exercised. Speakers from PagerDuty, Adobe, Google, Snowflake, ServiceNow, General Motors, Harness and a crowd of observability vendors showed what to measure instead.

Green is a claim, not a proof

Diamond sponsor Harness opened with Uma Mukkara, head of resilience testing and LitmusChaos co-founder, on why dashboards can only show paths that have already run. His case study is a third-party API failing over to a redundant path that never carried traffic, a retry storm turning a partial outage into a full one, and a team debugging an hour nobody instrumented. The cure is an inventory of untested paths and controlled experiments to fill it.

Eleftheria Batsou (UptimeRobot) took the outside-in version: your app returns a healthy 200 while customers can't pay because Stripe is degraded. The thing that broke is the payment provider, the identity provider, the CDN or the LLM API you added last quarter. Victoria Nduka (VictoriaMetrics) proposed accessibility as a fifth golden signal, so regressions show up in SLOs instead of in an audit weeks later. And Sylvain Kalache (Rootly) pointed the same discipline at people: we have liveness probes for every service, but the engineer holding the pager gets "How are you doing?" and always answers "Fine."

Agents need traces of their own

The busiest track was agent observability. Sabith K Soopy (Stackgen) put it best in one line of his abstract: traditional APM won't tell you an agent burned 40k tokens narrating a wrong answer. He showed the spans Stackgen uses to follow an agent through plan, gather and present, with per-tool cost and latency. Emerson Braun (Plan A Technologies) followed one agent run from request to outcome and instrumented the context it received, the decisions it made and where it started to drift.

Elliot Gardiner (Code Telemetry) treated coding agents as long-running processes that search, edit, test, retry and delegate to subagents, and argued that token counts and adoption are the wrong metrics for them. Princewill Kalio (Dockie) said the quiet part out loud in his title: AI systems are distributed systems now, with retrieval pipelines, vector stores and background workers, and they deserve distributed-systems tracing rather than print statements.

The 3am page for code no human wrote

Two talks dealt with the operational aftermath. Ralph Bird (PagerDuty) opens at 03:47 with a pager firing over code written by one agent, shipped by another, never seen by a human, after the SRE agent has already failed. Artemis Leonardou (NOFire AI) lived it: an agent-written change passed review and CI, then took a production path down for about three hours. Nothing in the diff was wrong on its own; the failure lived in the combination, and the dashboards could say what and where but not why.

Measuring whether the AI was right

Srikanth Devarakonda (Adobe) connected generative AI evaluation (factual accuracy, grounding, safety, task completion) to observable system performance and business outcomes instead of static benchmarks. Arjun D Sureshbabu (Snowflake) shared lessons from a human-in-the-loop architecture for legal, compliance and privacy NLP, where a hallucination has a regulatory cost. Ravi Chandra (Google) went after the semantic layer behind analytics agents, using feedback to keep a static, expert-curated ontology from missing the long tail of what users actually ask.

Pipelines, kernels and the bill

On the plumbing side, Anais Dotis (groundcover) gave a hype-free explanation of eBPF and how kernel programming escaped the kernel into monitoring and security. Rita Lopes (Gigapipe) started from the familiar four-backend stack of Prometheus, Loki, Tempo and Pyroscope, and the trade-off between observing everything and paying for it. Diana Todea (VictoriaMetrics) built a green observability pipeline entirely from open source and described how she got there by contributing upstream. Emmanuela Opurum (SoftNet Technologies) argued for designing observability into cloud architectures rather than bolting it on, and Joshua Fox (DoiT International) went beyond HPA and VPA for Kubernetes autoscaling that cuts waste without hurting reliability.

Telemetry as test input

Two talks turned signals into tests. Vasuki Uday Kiran Vudathala (ServiceNow) replaced interviews and spreadsheet guesses about peak traffic with workload models built from observability data. Sumaiyya Fatima (General Motors) applied observability-driven validation to hardware-in-the-loop testing for software-defined vehicles, where functionality emerges from many domains talking to each other.

Sponsors and where to watch

entry.title: Green dashboards only show the paths you have already tested
entry.summary: Uma Mukkara of Harness at Conf42 Observability 2026 on why green dashboards can't prove resilience, and a four-step loop to test the untested paths.
entry.content:
Your dashboards can only show the paths your system has actually walked. At Conf42 Observability 2026, Uma Mukkara, who leads resilience testing at Harness and co-founded LitmusChaos and OpenEBS, argued that the fallback route, the retry path and the DR plan are exactly the ones nobody instrumented, and that the only way to see them is to break things on purpose first.

The keynote is short and practical. It is also a Harness talk: the last section demos Harness Resilience Testing. The first two thirds stand on their own as an argument for any observability team.

The gap is widening, and he names three accelerants

The premise: the observability system says green, and incidents keep happening anyway. Not one or two, but a steady stream in large organisations. Mukkara blames three accelerants. Systems keep getting more distributed and dynamic, with more dependencies. Releases happen all the time, and AI-assisted coding has pushed some teams to tens of releases a day. And agents are now in the loop, which brings a failure shape of its own.

Observability, in his framing, tells you what is happening. It does not tell you what would happen.

Four things a dashboard never shows

He lists the blind spots plainly:

  • Single points of failure. A dashboard shows what is instrumented and exercised. An untested dependency stays invisible until it goes.
  • Timeouts and retries that trigger new paths. The code has been green for months because that branch never ran.
  • Degraded mode. If the system has never been degraded, nobody knows what degraded looks like on screen.
  • Recovery. If you never ran a DR test, you have no idea what your dashboards will say during one.

The uncomfortable part is timing. These are precisely the dashboards you need when a single point of failure trips, timeouts pile up and the system drops into degraded mode or DR.

A retry storm in a path that never carried traffic

His case study is the pattern most on-call engineers will recognise. Everything is green. A third-party API stops responding, and the system fails over to a redundant path that has never carried traffic, so nobody instrumented it. Retries on the new path turn a partial outage into a full one within the next thirty minutes to an hour, and when the full outage lands, the team is debugging blind because nothing captured that hour.

The fix he prescribes is boring in the best way: find that failover path ahead of time, exercise it in a lower environment, and build the dashboards for it before production needs them.

Agents can report healthy while doing the wrong thing

The new failure shape is the AI agent. A health check can return 200 OK while the model behind it is slow but not down, and Mukkara's point is that a slow model is as bad as a broken one. A tool call can time out silently while the agent keeps answering 200. His suggestion: inject latency between the model endpoint and the agent and check whether your observability reports the agent's real health, or just its HTTP status.

The four-step loop

The method fits on an index card:

  1. Inventory tested versus untested paths. For every "what happens if this network fails", ask whether you have seen it or assumed it.
  2. Run controlled experiments with a small blast radius against the untested ones.
  3. Add the missing dashboards and metrics the experiments reveal.
  4. Repeat it, quarterly or more often.

For a next step he suggests starting with your most critical service, listing every assumption never observed in production, and putting your agentic systems into degraded mode to see if the dashboards tell the truth.

What the demo shows

The closing demo covers Harness Resilience Testing, which runs chaos experiments, load tests and DR tests from one place. AI-assisted risk scanners read deployment metadata, logs, configuration and runtime events to flag likely risks before you run anything, and a resilience testing agent recommends and creates the experiments to confirm them.

SREs and observability owners who have ever had to explain a green dashboard in a postmortem. Platform teams adding AI agents to production will get the most from the agent section, which is short but specific.

entry.title: Conf42 Remix 2026: 52 talks from every corner of the series
entry.summary: Conf42 Remix 2026 roundup: resilience, AI agents in production, Kubernetes GPUs, Go monoliths, security basics and accessible JavaScript in 52 talks.
entry.content:
Conf42 Remix 2026, on August 20, 2026, is the one event in the series that refuses to pick a topic. It brings together popular talks from across the Conf42 calendar, grouped into tracks named after the series' own conferences, from Rustlang and Golang to Incident Management, DevSecOps and Large Language Models. The 52 talks ranged from Spotify's scaling lessons to monitoring garden plants with IoT sensors, and the whole lineup is on the event page.

Here are the threads that ran across the tracks.

Resilience is a separate goal from uptime

Harness opened with a keynote from Uma Mukkara, Head of Resilience Testing and co-creator of LitmusChaos. His argument: reliability is about staying available, resilience is about how you come back when a provider fails underneath you, and SREs should push for resilience gates in the pipeline the way they already gate on test coverage. He closed with AI-generated resilience risk reports as a way to win permission for chaos testing.

Stuart Clark of Spotify told the story of hyper-growth in 2014 creating fragmentation that made onboarding and incident response harder, and the lesson that good abstractions teach complexity rather than hide it. Sylvain Kalache of Rootly looked at what LLM-assisted coding does to reliability, including AI-generated tests that mirror the bugs they should catch. Spiros Economakis of NOFire AI argued the real AI opportunity in SRE is customer-centred prevention rather than faster RCA, and cloud architect Renato Losio shared five hard lessons from five years of so-called serverless databases.

AI agents meet production constraints

Samuel Baruffi of AWS addressed why so many agent projects stall at proof of concept, and how Amazon Bedrock AgentCore covers identity, gateway-based tool access, runtime isolation and memory. Michael Levan of Solo.io focused on the two questions every team running MCP gets asked: how do we observe it, and how do we keep costs down?

Two talks went after the context problem. Roxane Fischer, co-founder of Anyshift.io, showed infrastructure modelled as a graph so an LLM can follow multi-hop dependencies with Graph RAG and natural-language-to-Cypher queries instead of guessing. Lior Schejter asked what happens when an agent that copes well with one repo meets a distributed system of 200 microservices, and how to give it a mental model of the whole. And Leo Visser of OGD ICT-diensten demonstrated API management as the leash that keeps AI usage, budget and risk under control.

Kubernetes as a platform for everything

Piotr Zaniewski of vCluster spun up multi-tenant sandboxes with NVIDIA's open-source KAI Scheduler inside them to share fractional GPUs between teams. Christophe Gigax of Hager Group made the case for Dapr as an abstraction layer for state, pub/sub and more. Peng Wang of OceanBase showed one database handling RAG, semantic search and log analytics on Kubernetes, and Alejandro Mercado of Michael Page covered eBPF-powered observability for root cause analysis in clusters.

Go and Rust, from monoliths to leaderboards

The Golang track had two strong engineering stories. Victor Lyuboslavsky of Fleet Device Management described modularising a 10-year-old Go monolith whose layers had turned into hidden coupling and unclear ownership, and was candid about the people side as well as the architecture. Ivan Balashov of SoftSwiss walked through a leaderboard system that suffered daily outages, and the redesign that took its core operation from O(N²) to O(log N). Emmanuela Opurum of SoftNet Technologies used Go to build secure CI/CD automation components. On the Rustlang track, Tashi Garg of Juniper Networks built dynamic infrastructure UIs in Rust.

Security fundamentals, explained well

Several talks were good introductions, and said so. Peter De Tender of Microsoft gave a lap around GitHub Dependabot, CodeQL and the other built-in security features. Safeer C M of MoEngage opened the black box of static analysis using open-source Semgrep. Security engineer Aleksandra Drobnjak set out a minimum viable set of ISO 42001 documents for anyone asked who approved an AI system and on what data, and Marat Kenzhebulatov of Booking.com showed how to bring AI agents safely into security-critical backend work like code review and threat modelling.

The web, data and one garden

Gian Wild of AccessibilityOz gave concrete code for accessible forms and JavaScript, reminding everyone that a fifth of the population has a disability. Daniel Afonso of PagerDuty reviewed a decade of change in JavaScript testing. Alejandro Duarte of MariaDB covered RAG in production, glue-on-pizza hallucinations included, and Maximilian Schattauer of Perelyn showed LLM-driven pairwise ranking beating semantic retrievers on hard document retrieval.

And for the weekend, Marie Cruz of Grafana Labs showed how to monitor soil moisture with IoT sensors and Grafana Cloud as a project to do with your kids. The only talk of the day where the alert means water the basil.

Sponsors

Thanks to Harness, our diamond sponsor, to gold sponsors SREday and LLMday, and to HockeyStick for the podcast partnership.

What's next

entry.title: Reliability keeps your job, resilience gets you promoted
entry.summary: Uma Mukkara of Harness, co-creator of LitmusChaos, at Conf42 Remix 2026 on resilience gates, SLIs in chaos experiments and AI risk reports.
entry.content:
Your provider will go down eventually; the question is whether you go down with it. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Uma Mukkara, Head of Resilience Testing at Harness and co-creator of the CNCF projects LitmusChaos and OpenEBS, made the case that SREs should treat resilience as a separate goal from reliability, test it inside the delivery pipeline, and use AI to make the business case for doing so.

Uma has spent years helping teams practise chaos engineering, and he is candid about why most don't: everyone agrees it matters, but they aren't allowed to run it. Much of this keynote is about getting that permission.

Reliability and resilience are different goals

Uma's opening distinction: reliability is about staying available, resilience is about how you behave and how fast you come back when something pushes you over. Your cloud provider, your CDN or a security agent update can all fail on a day when your own code is fine, and no number of nines on their SLA makes that impossible.

Resilience is controlling the blast radius when that happens. Does one region go down, or all of them? Do you have the runbooks, and are people trained on them? Do you understand the dependencies well enough to recover? He also had the line of the session for anyone writing a promotion packet: "If you want to keep your job, focus on reliability. If you want to get yourself promoted, focus on resilience." When a shared provider fails and you stay up while a competitor doesn't, that difference gets noticed.

Chaos engineering is how you find weaknesses

Uma pushes back on the idea that chaos engineering means breaking things on purpose. The goal is data about weaknesses. A known weakness is already valuable: you can prepare a recovery plan, or tell your most important customer about the risk before it bites, which he argues is often enough to keep that relationship intact.

He describes an experiment as two kinds of boxes. Fault injections are one; checks that the system is still healthy are the other. Real incidents rarely come from one fault, so good experiments chain them: a network path fails over, load shifts, a memory leak starts, and the second provider slows down at the same time.

The SRE's job is defining those health checks. Observability experts know which service level indicators matter in production, and that knowledge rarely makes it back to engineering. Hand over the SLIs and the blast radius map, and pre-production chaos tests start measuring the right things.

Put resilience gates in the pipeline

Pipelines already gate on test coverage and regressions. Uma asks why they don't gate on resilience: is this release more or less resilient than the last one? If production experiments are off the table, push for chaos tests in staging, then low-intensity game days in production, and escalate if the answer to both is no.

He offers a maturity scale to aim at. In his view most organisations have moved from level one to level two in recent years; the target is level three, where critical services go through chaos testing in lower environments and a few game days run every year. Fully autonomous resilience, he admits, nobody does yet.

AI writes the risk report for you

The third part is about AI, and it's where the product enters. Uma calls it passive risk detection: feed deployment, incident and service data to an LLM, for example through MCP, and ask for a resilience risk report without running a single experiment. A report that says risk has grown over the last few releases is something you can take to management.

He then describes Harness doing the same from Argo CD or Harness CD data: listing likely incidents and proposing the chaos experiments to run, generated from a prompt. Active testing then confirms what the passive scan suggested.

Who should watch

SREs who believe in chaos engineering but can't get it approved, and engineering managers deciding where resilience fits in the SDLC. If your team already runs regular game days with SLO-based checks, the AI section is the new material. Uma also gave this keynote at Conf42 SRE 2026.

Related Conf42 talks

  • Chaos Validation Made Easy: Plug & Play with Resilience Probes, the health-check half of an experiment, from the Harness chaos team.
  • Implementing Chaos Engineering in a Risk Averse Culture by Kyle Shelton (Toyota), on the permission problem.
  • Enhancing Hypothesis Development Through Resilience Modeling by Gunnar Grosch (AWS).

entry.title: Conf42 LLMs 2026 roundup: context, judges and voice agents
entry.summary: Conf42 Large Language Models 2026 in review, from agent memory and knowledge graphs to verifiers, voice pipelines under 500 ms and regulated AI.
entry.content:
By June 2026 nobody at Conf42 Large Language Models 2026 needed convincing that models can write code or answer questions. The 34 talks, streamed online on June 18, 2026, were about everything around the model: what context it sees, who checks its work, how fast it has to answer on a phone call, and how it behaves inside a bank's ledger. Speakers came from Harness, AWS, Revolut, Snowflake, Microsoft, Meta, Walmart, Expedia Group and a good number of startups.

The bottleneck is context, not capability

The keynote set the tone. Prateek Mittal, Director of Product Management at Harness, argued that the next limit on AI in software delivery is context, and showed a knowledge graph of services, pipelines, deployments and owners that an agent queried to find the pipelines failing most often and why.

Three other talks attacked the same problem from different angles. Anannya Roy Chowdhury (AWS) observed that agents in production rarely fail because they can't reason; they fail because they retrieve the wrong context. The talk's framework splits agent memory into working, retrieval and persistent layers. Lior Schejter described what happens when an agent meets 200 microservices instead of one repo: it gets lost in the middle. The fix is an AI-maintained architecture hub of APIs, domain models and events written for agents to read. Varun Joshi (AWS) made the data engineer's version of the case: your schema, lineage, query history and dbt models are the context, and most teams haven't wired them into RAG yet.

Who judges the agent?

Vsevolod Voropaev (Olo din) gave one of the sharper talks of the day: the verifier is the hardest component of an agentic system and usually the last one built. Drawing on a bandit-based verification layer routing across Claude, GPT and Gemini, he argued that verifiers should usually be smarter than the agents they watch. Liliya Imasheva and Michael Banf (Perelyn) showed a summary-validation pipeline that pairs BERTScore, ROUGE and BLEU with LLM-as-judge scoring on completeness, conciseness, harmlessness, correctness and readability.

Permissions were the other half of trust. Sohan Maheshwar (AuthZed) pointed out that letting a coding agent decide for itself what is safe is a probabilistic answer to a question that needs a deterministic one, and showed how to add enforceable permission boundaries. Neeraj Kumar Singh Beshane (Meta) presented RuntimeGuard-AI, which records tamper-evident, hash-chained evidence across an inference pipeline for EU AI Act compliance, and Arunkumar Muthuramalingam (General Reinsurance) treated IAM as the core of AI security.

Voice, phones and people who don't want an app

Voice agents got a strong cluster. Bohdan Snisar (Solea AI) started from the classic STT, LLM, TTS chain, where every stage waits for the last and the whole conversation turn has under 500 milliseconds. He built the pipeline up layer by layer, through realtime audio transport, voice activity detection and turn detection, to show where it hits the wall, then presented an architecture that reasons in parallel while the agent talks. Pavel Shchekotov (Denk Solutions) removed the app altogether and put an LLM agent behind an ordinary phone number for people who are sceptical of AI.

The most British title of the event belonged to Anton Denisov (Dwelly), whose system reads emails and calls for dissatisfaction that customers soften with politeness, understatement or silence. Anyone who has heard a British colleague call a plan 'brave' will appreciate the problem. Andrii Veremiienko (Revolut) brought the mobile view: latency, inference costs, rate limits and UX design around answers that aren't deterministic. Petras Bazdaras argued that when generating code is cheap, reading it is the skill that matters.

Shipping it: pipelines, modernisation and serving

Denis Ermakov (Tehpotok) presented an open-source framework for agent-driven CI/CD with retries, observability and explicit points where humans stay in the loop. Marco Antonio Silva (Microsoft) shared spec-driven modernisation with Spec2Cloud and the GitHub Copilot Modernization CLI, including a large project at a Portuguese financial institution. Tim Spann (Snowflake) showed Cortex Code managing schema changes and deployments from natural language.

On the serving side, Kosseila Haddalene (Cloudthrill) explained why diffusion transformers, which denoise instead of generating tokens and are compute-bound rather than memory-bound, are awkward to serve next to LLMs, and how vLLM-Omni handles both. Sergey Speranskiy covered the Kubernetes assumptions that break first under LLM workloads, Kandasamy Selvaraj (ADP) shifted RAG performance testing left into CI/CD, and Leo Visser (OGD ICT-diensten) put Azure API Management in front of models for content filtering, token-aware throttling and caching. Andrei Shcherbinin (Social Discovery Group) walked through a production automoderation stack that mixes lightweight classifiers with multimodal LLMs for grey areas.

LLMs in regulated systems

A large share of the programme dealt with finance, tax, healthcare and audit. Abdul Basit Iqbal (Amazon) turned changing tax regulations into executable compliance logic, Karishma Velisetty governed AI code assistants in SOX audit analytics, Ravindra Rajasekhar Kavuru (Expedia Group) built compliance into co-branded credit card apps, and Rakesh Jha (DXC Technology) applied LLMs to general ledgers. On the people side, Lakshmi Priya Gopalsamy made the point that as AI speeds up execution, human decision capacity becomes the constraint, and Susanta Kumar Sahoo looked at LLM copilots for incident response.

Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to Harness and LLMday, the diamond sponsors, to the Prompt Engineering Conference as gold sponsor, to HockeyStick as podcast partner, and to the media partners. The full Conf42 LLMs 2026 playlist has every talk, and the event page lists them by track.

Next up in the series is Conf42 Large Language Models 2027.

entry.title: Shipping with Context: Knowledge Graphs as the Backbone of AI-First Software Delivery
entry.summary: Shipping with Context: Why Knowledge Graphs Are Becoming the Backbone of AI-First Software Delivery AI is transforming software development at an extraordinary pace. Developers can generate code, wri
entry.content:
Shipping with Context: Why Knowledge Graphs Are Becoming the Backbone of AI-First Software Delivery

AI is transforming software development at an extraordinary pace. Developers can generate code, write tests, create documentation, and troubleshoot issues faster than ever before.

Yet for most organizations, the real challenge is no longer generating code.

The harder problem is understanding context.

A piece of generated code does not exist in isolation. It interacts with services, infrastructure, security controls, deployment pipelines, compliance requirements, operational processes, and business objectives. Without understanding those relationships, AI systems may be capable of producing outputs, but they struggle to make reliable decisions.

In his session Shipping with Context: Knowledge Graphs as the Backbone of AI-First Software Delivery, Prateek Mittal explored why context is emerging as the next critical layer of enterprise AI and why knowledge graphs are becoming a foundational component of modern software delivery systems.

The Next AI Bottleneck Is Not Model Capability

Over the past few years, the conversation around AI has largely focused on model performance.

Organizations compare models, benchmark reasoning capabilities, and evaluate new generations of large language models.

However, many enterprises are discovering that model quality is no longer the primary limitation.

The real bottleneck is access to organizational context.

Most enterprises operate across dozens or hundreds of systems:

  • CI/CD platforms
  • Security tools
  • Cloud infrastructure
  • Observability platforms
  • Ticketing systems
  • Source control repositories
  • Incident management platforms
  • Cost management tools

Each system contains valuable information.

The challenge is that this information remains fragmented.

An AI assistant may understand how to write code, but it often lacks visibility into which services are affected by that code, which teams own those services, what policies apply to them, and what business risks might be introduced by a deployment.

Without context, intelligence remains limited.

Why Enterprise AI Struggles With Context

The problem is not simply a lack of data.

Most organizations already have enormous amounts of operational information available.

The challenge is that this information exists inside disconnected systems.

As Mittal explained, enterprise AI initiatives frequently encounter four common obstacles.

Data Silos

Critical information is distributed across numerous platforms and tools.

Even when the data exists, it is often inaccessible to AI systems or difficult to connect across domains.

Missing Domain Knowledge

General-purpose language models understand public information but typically lack awareness of company-specific terminology, workflows, ownership structures, and operational practices.

This creates a gap between what AI knows and what an organization actually needs.

Hallucination Risk

When models lack context, they compensate by making assumptions.

These assumptions can produce inaccurate recommendations, incorrect conclusions, or actions based on incomplete information.

Governance and Compliance Concerns

Organizations must carefully control how sensitive information is accessed and shared.

Providing AI systems with unrestricted access to enterprise data can introduce security, compliance, and governance risks.

Together, these challenges limit the ability of AI systems to operate effectively in production environments.

The Evolution From AI-Assisted DevOps to AI-Operational DevOps

Many teams are already using AI in their software delivery processes.

Most of these implementations fall into what Mittal describes as AI-assisted DevOps.

In this model, AI helps humans perform tasks such as:

  • Writing code
  • Creating configuration files
  • Generating documentation
  • Producing runbooks
  • Answering operational questions

Humans remain responsible for supplying context, validating outputs, and making final decisions.

This approach delivers productivity gains, but it does not fundamentally change how software delivery operates.

A second model is beginning to emerge.

What Is AI-Operational DevOps?

AI-operational DevOps shifts AI from being a productivity tool to becoming an active participant in delivery workflows.

Instead of requiring humans to manually provide context, AI systems automatically retrieve information from shared enterprise models.

This allows agents to:

  • Evaluate deployment risks
  • Analyze dependencies
  • Simulate outcomes
  • Enforce policies
  • Validate compliance requirements
  • Recommend corrective actions

In this model, context becomes machine-readable rather than conversational.

The system itself becomes responsible for understanding relationships and applying guardrails before actions occur.

This transition requires a shared understanding of the software delivery ecosystem.

That is where knowledge graphs enter the picture.

Understanding the Building Blocks of a Knowledge Graph

A knowledge graph is not simply a database or reporting system.

It is a representation of entities and the relationships between them.

Within a software delivery environment, entities may include:

  • Services
  • Pipelines
  • Deployments
  • Incidents
  • Infrastructure resources
  • Cloud costs
  • Security findings
  • Teams
  • Applications

These entities become nodes within the graph.

The relationships between them become edges.

For example:

  • A service depends on another service
  • A deployment originates from a specific commit
  • A pipeline belongs to a particular team
  • An incident affects a specific application
  • A cloud resource supports a particular workload

Individually, each piece of information has limited value.

Connected together, they create a model that describes how an organization actually operates.

Context Is More Than Data

One of the key ideas presented during the session is that context is not merely information.

Context is information combined with relationships.

Many organizations already collect deployment events, operational metrics, cloud costs, and security findings.

The challenge is that these data points often remain disconnected.

A knowledge graph introduces a semantic layer that allows systems to understand how information relates across domains.

This transforms isolated records into an interconnected model of software delivery.

Instead of querying a single tool, AI systems can reason across multiple systems simultaneously.

Building a Knowledge Graph for Software Delivery

Creating a useful knowledge graph requires more than importing data.

Organizations must establish a process for constructing and maintaining relationships.

The process generally includes several stages.

Entity Extraction

The first step is identifying important objects within the delivery ecosystem.

These may include applications, services, incidents, deployments, users, cloud resources, or security findings.

Metadata Enrichment

Entities become more valuable when supplemented with additional information.

Examples include:

  • Ownership details
  • Team assignments
  • Version information
  • Environment data
  • Compliance classifications
  • Security policies

Relationship Mapping

Relationships define how entities interact.

Understanding who owns a service, which deployment modified it, and what infrastructure supports it is often more valuable than understanding any individual component in isolation.

Query Exposure

Once the graph exists, APIs and query interfaces allow AI agents to retrieve and reason about context dynamically.

At that point, the graph becomes an operational system rather than simply a data repository.

Why Knowledge Graph Projects Fail

Knowledge graphs have existed for years, yet many implementations struggle to deliver value.

According to Mittal, the most common failure is not technical.

It is a failure of use case definition.

Organizations sometimes invest heavily in building sophisticated graph models without clearly identifying the problems they intend to solve.

This creates several risks.

Over-Modeling

Teams create highly detailed ontologies that are technically impressive but provide little practical value.

The result is significant complexity with limited adoption.

Under-Modeling

The opposite problem occurs when relationships are not modeled deeply enough.

Data remains connected only superficially, preventing meaningful reasoning.

Stale Context

A graph is only valuable if it reflects reality.

Outdated relationships and stale metadata quickly reduce the usefulness of AI-driven decision-making.

Successful implementations focus on solving specific operational challenges rather than building graphs for their own sake.

How Knowledge Graphs Enable AI Reasoning

One of the most compelling aspects of knowledge graphs is their ability to support complex reasoning across multiple systems.

During the session, Mittal demonstrated how AI could analyze software delivery pipelines across an organization and identify patterns that would be difficult to discover manually.

Rather than searching individual projects one at a time, the system was able to reason across organizational boundaries.

The AI identified:

  • Pipelines with the highest failure rates
  • Common failure patterns
  • Missing dependencies
  • Configuration issues
  • Potential remediation actions

The system not only surfaced operational problems but also suggested corrective actions based on the relationships captured inside the graph.

This illustrates a broader shift in how AI interacts with enterprise systems.

Instead of responding only to direct questions, AI can begin to understand operational context and assist with diagnosis, prioritization, and decision-making.

Shared Context Across Engineering Disciplines

The value of a knowledge graph extends far beyond DevOps.

Modern software delivery requires collaboration across multiple domains.

DevOps teams care about deployments and reliability.

SecOps teams focus on vulnerabilities and compliance.

FinOps teams analyze cloud spending and resource utilization.

Platform engineering teams manage infrastructure and developer experience.

Traditionally, each group operates within its own set of tools and dashboards.

Knowledge graphs provide a shared context layer that connects these perspectives.

When everyone operates against the same model of services, dependencies, ownership, and operational events, decision-making becomes faster and more consistent.

Governance Becomes a Core AI Requirement

As AI systems gain access to broader organizational context, governance becomes increasingly important.

Enterprise AI cannot operate solely on trust.

Systems require mechanisms for:

  • Role-based access control
  • Policy enforcement
  • Auditability
  • Compliance validation
  • Permission management

Knowledge graphs provide the contextual foundation that allows these controls to be applied consistently.

Without governance, increased context introduces risk.

With governance, context becomes a strategic advantage.

The Future of AI-First Software Delivery

The software industry has spent years building increasingly capable AI models.

The next phase of adoption will depend less on model intelligence and more on organizational context.

The most successful AI systems will not necessarily be those with the largest parameter counts.

They will be the systems that understand services, dependencies, ownership, policies, infrastructure, incidents, and business priorities.

Knowledge graphs provide a mechanism for connecting these elements into a unified model.

As AI moves from assisting developers to actively participating in software delivery workflows, shared context will become essential infrastructure.

Context Is the New Competitive Advantage

Software delivery is becoming increasingly complex.

Organizations operate across dozens of platforms, hundreds of services, and thousands of interconnected components.

AI has the potential to help manage this complexity, but only if it can understand the environment in which it operates.

Knowledge graphs offer a way to transform fragmented organizational knowledge into a connected, queryable system that both humans and AI can reason about.

In an AI-first future, the question will no longer be whether models can generate answers.

The question will be whether they have enough context to generate the right ones.

entry.title: Conf42 Database DevOps 2026: migrations, operators and AI on call
entry.summary: Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 roundup - safe schema migrations, a 30-day Kubernetes operator test, serverless database lessons and AI-assisted tuning.
entry.content:
Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 ran online on June 4, 2026, with 25 talks about the part of the stack that does not roll back cleanly. The schedule was split into AI, automation, delivery, governance, and scale tracks, but one question ran through all of them: now that AI can write your migrations and tune your queries, which parts of database operations can you safely hand over, and which still need a human with a pager?

Every talk is on the Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 event page and in the YouTube playlist.

The riskiest deploy you ship

Schema migrations got the most attention, and for good reason. Ahmed Tariq, a Cloud DevOps Engineer, opened his abstract with the line every DBA nods at: application releases can be rolled forward and back, but a migration that locks a 2TB table for an hour, or quietly loses data on rollback, cannot. His field guide covers expand-and-contract, migration tests, approval gates, and post-deploy checks, then adds AI where it earns its keep (drafting forward and rollback DDL, flagging unsafe operations) and is honest about where it breaks, such as hallucinated Postgres flags that are really MySQL flags.

Diamond sponsor Harness showed the pattern end to end. Stephen Atwell, Director of Product at Harness, had AI write a trigger-based Postgres migration that splits a JSON blob column into real columns, then shipped it through blue-green in staging and canary in production with no downtime, with policy checks, production data cloned to staging, and an AI-written test confirming that both app versions saw the same orders.

Niraj Katkamwar of Intuit presented independent research on a prompt-driven framework that turns natural-language requirements into microservice and schema changes.

Can the operator replace the DBA?

Amarachi Iheanacho of SideroLabs ran the experiment many teams argue about but never run: hand day-to-day operations of a PostgreSQL cluster to the CloudNativePG operator for 30 days, then deliberately inject node failures, pod crashes, storage pressure, replication issues, upgrades, and restores. Some problems were fixed automatically within seconds; others needed a human. The week-by-week walkthrough is the most honest answer to the title you will find.

Renato Losio brought five lessons from five years of so-called serverless databases on AWS. He once drew the New York City skyline with Aurora Serverless v2 capacity at re:Invent, and says fifteen years with AWS does not make him an expert, it just makes him old. Among them: serverless is just an adjective, and storage usually matters more than CPU. His key message: serverless databases remove capacity management, but they don't remove database engineering.

AI as the junior DBA

Several talks put AI into the tuning loop. Naga Bellamkonda of Gartner and Ellavarasan Asokan of Capital One, both long-time Oracle and Postgres administrators, shared lessons from AI-driven optimisation in production, from predictive tuning towards more autonomous operations. Sampath Rao Madarapu of Microsoft showed Copilot in Azure for diagnostics and resource control.

On the AI application side, Alejandro Duarte of MariaDB covered RAG in production, starting from the infamous glue-on-pizza answers, and Ankur Aggarwal of Meta tackled a hard gap: how an LLM running in a trusted execution environment can query databases through MCP without exposing sensitive data.

Same SQL, different answers

The governance track had the talk most data engineers should watch. Muthupalaniappan Ramanathan of DoorDash showed how identical queries can return different results on Spark, Trino, and Snowflake because of type handling, null semantics, and optimiser behaviour, and proposed a canonical semantic layer with CI-integrated validation to catch the drift.

Sheena Yap Chan argued that the real risk is often not missing data but database signals that never reach the right people in time. Muthu Saravanan of Mind-Pros and Dharmendra Ahuja of IBM looked at intentional delivery and ethical validation inside AI-driven data pipelines.

Always on, at scale

The scale track was heavy on finance. Priyatham Nagaiya Seenu Naidu of Mastercard covered real-time payment networks like FedNow, UPI, PIX, and SEPA Instant, where the database must be up around the clock with sub-second processing. Ritvik Pandya of JPMorgan Chase started from a sudden p99 spike at peak hours and traced it to the ingress layer, fixing it with deterministic routing for cache locality. Srikanth Uddanti of Charles Schwab walked through the trade-offs of distributed databases, and Surya Lankalapalli of Microsoft made the case for active-active, multi-provider DNS, the dependency that quietly delays database failover.

Elsewhere in the lineup: Jason Lester of Capgemini on loading cloud API output into a database for analysis the console cannot do, Sulabh Jain on modernising insurance core systems, Sirisha Ayyagari of IBM on real-time SAP pricing, Kamini Murugaboopathy on real-time marketing analytics, Bharat Kumar Reddy Karumuri of General Motors on operationalising ML and GenAI, Zeeshan Khan on hiring as a data infrastructure problem, and Harsha Vardhani Talluri on multi-vendor DOCSIS deployments.

Sponsors and what's next
